messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Conflict: Confrontations, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event

Vignette:
Marcus Holt is a 49-year-old plumber who has been married for eleven years and who, until recently, managed to keep the worst of what had happened to him pressed down beneath the ordinary weight of a working day. He presented for intake following what he described as "a breaking point" — a moment at a job site three weeks prior that left him shaking in his truck for nearly an hour, unable to return to work for the rest of the afternoon.

The events that brought Marcus to therapy occurred approximately two years ago, during a relationship that preceded his current marriage. His partner at the time had a volatile temperament that escalated over the course of eighteen months into repeated episodes of physical violence. The incident that Marcus identifies as the most severe took place in her kitchen. An argument had begun quietly — he remembers her voice staying almost controlled at first, measured in a way that, he now understands, was its own kind of warning — before she struck him with a cast-iron pan that had been left on the burner. The pan had been heating. The smell of scorched metal and the faint acrid trace of burnt residue on the iron filled the room. He remembers that smell more precisely than he remembers her face in that moment. He suffered a laceration to his forearm and a fractured wrist. He did not call the police. He told his employer he had slipped on a wet floor.

In the months following, Marcus met his current wife, left the previous relationship entirely, and attempted to move forward. For a time, this appeared to work. But the symptoms that have since accumulated tell a different story. He finds himself unable to sleep at a normal hour, staying up well past midnight most nights, sitting in front of the television or scrolling his phone until exhaustion overtakes him. He cannot easily say why, only that going to bed earlier feels wrong in a way he struggles to articulate. He has also worked hard not to think about what happened — not to let his mind settle on the kitchen, the pan, the sequence of events — and has largely structured his inner life around avoiding that territory. He has not returned to the neighborhood where the apartment was located, rerouting his drives across that part of the city even when it adds twenty minutes to a job.

At work, the triggers have become harder to manage. Plumbing frequently takes Marcus into residential kitchens, and on the afternoon that finally brought him to seek help, he was repairing a pipe beneath a sink when a homeowner left something on the stove and the faint smell of scorched metal drifted through the room. He was back in that kitchen before he had any choice in the matter — not as a memory he was reviewing but as something happening to him now, immediate and physical. He made an excuse and left.

Confrontations on job sites have also become significant. When a general contractor raised his voice at Marcus over a scheduling dispute last spring — not aggressively, Marcus acknowledged, just firmly — Marcus found himself unable to respond, his chest tightening, his thoughts scattering. He had come to believe that any expression of anger in his vicinity, even calm displeasure, carries within it the possibility of sudden escalation. A colleague who snapped irritably at a supplier. A customer who expressed frustration about a delayed repair. Each instance lands in Marcus with a force that seems to him disproportionate but also, privately, entirely logical. He had learned, in that relationship, that quiet anger was simply loud anger with the volume turned down.

His wife has noticed that he seems unreachable at times, and that he flinches at things she cannot identify. He has told her very little. He had come to believe that speaking about what happened would mean confirming something about himself that he prefers to leave unexamined — that he was a man to whom this had been done. What he hopes for, sitting in the waiting room before his first session, is less clear to him than what he fears: that the telling of it will make it more real, not less.
